title: Nearly All of It Is Waiting
aliases: What’s Left When It Runs Out
logline: A hundred-and-sixty-foot brick and granite tower on the southernmost point of an island, built by an empire out of stone shipped from two quarries on the other side of the world, whose entire output is the few seconds in which a particular ship is in a particular place, and whose remaining time — almost all of it — is spent keeping accurate.
human_question: If the part of a thing that does the work is a few seconds in a night, what is all the rest of it doing, and why would we call that nothing?

place.what_kind_of_place: A low rocky point at the southern limit of an island, where the land stops in flat black rock and shallow surf and the horizon runs uninterrupted through more than half a circle. On the point stands one thing: an octagonal white brick tower of seven floors with a gallery and a lantern at the top, the tallest of its kind in the country, still a working aid to navigation and still owned and run by a national ports authority. Its lower courses are dressed granite that was quarried in Scotland and in Cornwall and brought here by sea; its bricks and its ironwork came from England. Around the base: a walled compound, a service building, a cable run, coconut palms bent inland by the monsoon, and a village of the same name a few hundred metres off. Nothing else on the point is tall. Nothing else on the point moves.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: One vertical object against an open horizon, at night, for a very long time. The tower is white, the sky is black, and every five seconds the lantern flashes and the whole shape reappears. In a held frame that is a rhythm a viewer settles into within a minute and then stops counting, and it goes on and on. The horizon is not decoration: from this point the sea fills the frame in three directions, and a long way out, in the busiest east–west shipping lane in this ocean, the lights of ships cross the frame for two or three minutes each and disappear. In daylight the same tower is a plain white column on black rock with surf at the bottom of it, and at close range it is a surface: salt, paint over paint, the grain of imported granite, glass. The film is built on shots in which nothing happens for minutes at a time, and the point is that the viewer can feel exactly how long that is.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Almost nothing, on purpose. The flash, on a fixed period of five seconds, which is the only clock in the film. The sea state, which on this coast is a different sea in the south-west monsoon than it is in the calm months, and which nobody controls. Ships, which arrive in the frame from outside it and leave the same way, at intervals nobody can schedule. The light going on at dusk and off at dawn. Weather across the horizon. Salt drying. That is the entire inventory of change, and the film does not add to it: the camera does not move, the edit does not cut for pace, and no shot is shortened because nothing is happening in it.
place.when_it_looks_best: Night is the film. A moonless clear night for the flash against black, a moonlit one for the tower to have a visible profile in the same frame as its own light. Dusk and dawn for the switch-on and the switch-off, which are the two events of the day. The calm season between the monsoons, roughly December to March on this coast, for a workable sea and for any seaward angle at all; the south-west monsoon gives a bigger, uglier, more interesting sea and takes the boat away.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A tower, a sea and a light, in that order, for the length of one night. It opens on a black frame in which something white flashes every five seconds and resolves into an enormous vertical object standing on the edge of an ocean. It goes close: cut granite, salt, layers of paint, the glass of a lantern. It goes wide again and holds, and somewhere in the middle of that hold a ship's lights enter at one edge of the frame, cross, and leave, and the tower does not react. Then dawn, the light goes out, and the same object is revealed as an ordinary white column on wet rock with the sea doing what it always does. Someone who never hears a word of the narration gets a complete piece with a beginning, a middle and a payoff — dark to light, far to near to far, one flash to one ship to one morning — and the thing they will remember is how long the shots were and how little needed to happen in them.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes an argument about proportion. The sources name fourteen jobs a moment of mind can do, and the nineteen minds that do the background job do it more often than anything else happens, and it is never felt [C034-P:L27–L29; C034-M:L41]. They say that whenever no new object is being taken, that background current is what is running, and that when something does arrive it breaks, an episode runs, and afterwards the current starts again [C034-P:L65]. They give the full sequence for the strongest kind of seeing and put light among the four conditions that all have to be strong at once [C041-P:L25; C041-P:L29–L48]. And they say that the early, receiving part of that sequence carries no wish to do anything at all and arises without effort, by the order of mind [C029-M:L3; C025-P:L75]. That is the shape of this building. Its output is a few seconds per ship; its condition of working is the rest. The voice never calls the tower a mind, never calls the light attention, and never turns any of this into a virtue: a light that has not failed is a fact about maintenance.

sequence.on_screen: Black. Something white flashes, once, and vanishes. Five seconds. Again. The camera does not move and the shot does not cut for a long time. Slowly the eye assembles a vertical shape around the flash: a tower, enormous, with nothing beside it.
sequence.voice: The old analysis counts fourteen jobs a moment of mind can do, and it names them in an order [C034-P:L27–L29]. Nineteen kinds of mind share three of those jobs between them, and they only ever do one at a time [C034-M:L45]. Two of the three happen once in a life. The third happens more than anything else, and the sources say plainly that it is never felt [C034-M:L41].

sequence.on_screen: First light, static, wide. The tower entire, white, on black rock, with surf at the foot of it and an empty horizon behind. Then closer, still static: dressed granite courses at the base, the joints, the paint, the ironwork of the gallery.
sequence.voice: This was built by the British at the end of the eighteen-eighties. Sir James Nicholas Douglass drew it and a Douglass built it, and the stone was not local: granite was selected at Dalbeattie in Scotland and at Penryn in Cornwall and brought here by sea, with the brick and the steel out of England. None of that was chosen for the moment of use. It was chosen so the thing would still be exactly here, and exactly this tall, a century later.

sequence.on_screen: Full day. The lantern is dark. One long static frame, held well past comfort: the tower, the rock, the sea, a palm moving slightly. Nothing enters the frame. Nothing leaves it.
sequence.voice: The background job has one description in the texts, and it is not a poetic one: to support the uninterrupted continuation of the life. Whenever no mind is arising that takes an object, this is what is running; when an object does turn up the current breaks, an episode runs, and when the episode is finished the current starts again [C034-P:L65]. Its own object is carried over and is described as unapparent — there, and not showing [C034-P:L73].

sequence.on_screen: Dusk. The lantern comes on: the first flash while there is still colour in the sky. Then the gallery in silhouette, and the horizon going. If the optic still turns and the air is thick enough to carry it, the beam itself sweeping out over the water.
sequence.voice: For the fullest kind of seeing the sources require four things to be strong at the same moment: a working eye, something there to be seen, light, and the mind turned that way [C041-P:L25]. Of the four, light is the only one anyone has ever had to build. Then the whole sequence runs — the current wavers, breaks, turns toward it, sees, receives, examines, settles, and only after that does anything get done [C041-P:L29–L48].

sequence.on_screen: The working parts, whatever proves filmable: mains cable and conduit, a generator housing, a switch, the inside of a painted stairwell if there is entry, the compound wall and the service door if there is not. Static, unhurried, no commentary in the framing.
sequence.voice: Seven factors run in every mind there is, without exception [C025-P:L47]. But of the six that come and go, effort is absent from sixteen of these early minds altogether, and the reason given is flat: they arise by the ordinary order of mind, without effort [C025-P:L75]. This framework does not hand out marks for effort or for drive. It is describing a machine, not praising one.

sequence.on_screen: Very close. Salt on glass. The lens or the lamp panel from directly below. A rusted bolt head, a painted number, the join between two blocks of imported granite. Held, one shot at a time, in silence.
sequence.voice: The receiving stages are sorted into five groups, and the differences between them are tiny — a factor here, a factor there [C029-P:L31–L55]. The barest one, the seeing itself, has only the seven, and the other forty-five do not occur in it at all [C029-P:L35]. And not one of these minds contains a wish to do anything [C029-M:L3]. The texts call them weak. That is a count of what they carry, and it is not a word about anybody.

sequence.on_screen: The longest hold in the film. Full dark, static, wide: the flashing tower on the left of frame, an open black sea filling the rest. Two or three minutes in, the lights of a ship enter at one edge, cross the frame without hurrying, and leave at the other. The tower does not change. The shot continues after the ship has gone.
sequence.voice: Forty thousand ships a year go past this point, and the useful part of what this building does for any one of them lasts about as long as you have just watched. The texts put the doing of an action, and its merit or its absence, in the short run of moments after the thing has been settled — not in the turning toward, not in the seeing [C034-M:L41]. Calling that the place a person responds is this series' framing and not the texts' wording. What the texts are exact about is the proportion.

sequence.on_screen: Dawn. The lantern goes out. One static frame of the same tower, now plainly white, on wet black rock, with a working sea. Held. A fishing boat somewhere far out. Nothing else.
sequence.voice: The sources end the episode and start the background again, and that is all they say happens next [C041-P:L48]. Nothing was revealed by the dark and nothing was taken away by the morning. This thing is not steady, and it is not patient, and it is not watching. It has been kept in working order by people who were paid to do it, and a light that has never failed is a fact about maintenance.

concept_merge.why_together: C034 is the film. Its digest gives the fourteen functions and their order, and the rule that a mind does one job at a time [C034-P:L27–L29; C034-M:L45] — but the load-bearing sentence is the census. In one life there is exactly one rebirth-linking mind and exactly one death mind; what arises abundantly is the life-continuum, and its arising is not felt; and the doing of actions, with merit and demerit, belongs to the impulsion moments [C034-M:L41]. The Pradeepika then says what the life-continuum function actually is: the support of the uninterrupted continuation of the existence, running at all times when no mind is arising that takes an object, breaking when one does, and starting again when the episode is over [C034-P:L65]; its object is inherited and unapparent, and the same nineteen minds that link a birth also do this [C034-P:L67; C034-P:L73]. So the mind-stream the sources describe is overwhelmingly made of a function whose whole job is accurate continuation, punctuated by short episodes in which anything is actually done. That is not an analogy for this building; it is its specification. A landfall light exists for the few seconds in which a particular vessel is in a particular place, and everything else it does — standing in the surveyed position, holding the focal plane, keeping the period, being repainted, being powered — is the condition of those seconds being right. C041 supplies the episode at full length: the seventeen moments for a very great object, and the four conditions that must all be strong together, one of which is light [C041-P:L25; C041-P:L29–L48]. Light is the only one of the four that anybody has ever had to manufacture, which is why a lighthouse can carry this concept without being turned into a symbol. C025 and C029 supply the workforce underneath. The seven universals run in every mind without exception [C025-P:L47; C025-M:L5]; the ten sense-consciousnesses get only those seven and none of the six occasional factors [C025-P:L59]; effort does not arise in sixteen of the rootless minds because they come about by the ordinary order of mind without effort [C025-P:L75]; the eighteen carry no unwholesome or beautiful factor and are therefore called weak [C029-P:L29]; and none of them contains a desire to act at all [C029-M:L3; C025-P:L87]. That is a neutral machinery that runs the same under any administration, which is exactly why this location's colonial construction is recorded and not argued about.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That waiting is not the absence of the work; it is the larger part of the work, and it is the part with no wanting in it. C034 alone is a table of jobs. C041 alone is an order of events. C025 alone is a map of where six neutral qualities turn up, and C029 alone is a table of what the receiving stages carry. Put on one tower they produce a proportion nobody can argue with, because the building was costed and engineered around it: imported granite and imported brick, the dues of two other lighthouses, a lens made for landfall, all of it spent on a handful of seconds per ship. The pairing also closes off the reading the concepts do not license. Nothing here is vigilance, nothing here is steadiness of character, and nothing here is a technique: the sources say the background moments are never felt and that countless moments pass in a finger-snap [C034-P:L37], so no viewer is invited to watch their own. The film ends on the least flattering true sentence available — the light has not failed because it has been maintained.

concept_links.why: The digest earns this location structurally rather than poetically. It names the fourteen functions and their order and the rule that each mind does one job at a time [C034-P:L27–L29; C034-M:L45]; it reports the census that decides the film — one rebirth-linking mind and one death mind in a whole life, the life-continuum arising abundantly and unfelt, and action with its merit or demerit sitting in the impulsion moments [C034-M:L41]; and it describes the life-continuum function itself as the support of unbroken continuation, present whenever no object is being taken, broken when one is, and resumed when the episode ends [C034-P:L65], with an inherited object the source calls unapparent and the same nineteen minds doing it as do the birth-linking [C034-P:L67; C034-P:L73]. A working landfall light is the same proportion in a building: an output measured in seconds per ship, and a remaining life whose entire content is keeping the output correct. The digest's limits are written into the film. It is not a mindfulness technique of watching each step, because the source says countless moments pass in a finger-snap [C034-P:L37] and the background moments are never felt, so no beat invites a viewer to observe their own. The background current is not a subconscious and not a hidden self, and beat 3 says only what the text says: a function, an object, and no noticing. Rebirth-linking is meant literally in the source and is not borrowed as a metaphor for a fresh start or a new beginning of any kind — nothing in this film is a beginning. The slogan about freedom living in the gap between stimulus and response is not used, because the digest says the source describes no conscious pause for weighing options; beat 7 states outright that reading impulsion as the place a person responds is the series' framing and not the text's wording. And the Pradeepika's link between weak rebirth-producing action and being born blind or deaf [C034-P:L47] is kept out of the film entirely, in voice, caption and research.

The digest reads the rootless table as a sequence and supplies what runs under the episode. The eighteen rootless minds carry only ethically variable factors, never an unwholesome or a beautiful one, and the source explains their weakness by the absence of roots [C029-P:L29]; across the five groupings the machinery gains only a little at each step, with effort appearing for the first time at the determining moment [C029-P:L31–L55; C029-P:L49; C029-M:L5–L9]; the barest of them, the seeing itself, has only the seven universals and the other forty-five factors do not occur [C029-P:L35]; and the Margaya states the ceiling up front — in rootless minds only twelve of the variable factors occur, desire-to-act excepted [C029-M:L3]. That is what lets a film about a machine hold six minutes of nothing without the voice smuggling intention into the object. The guards are carried exactly. 'No wish to act in the early stages' is not 'we have no free will' and not 'we are just machines' — the source puts wanting and moral quality in the later stage rather than nowhere, and beat 6 says so in the same breath. 'Rootless minds are weak' is a technical count of factors and beat 6 says that too, in as many words, because this film has a colonial engineering record in it and the word must not land on any person, any workforce or any nation. The factor counts are a student's aid and never appear on screen as measurements. And the fully freed person's smile-producing mind — the richest rootless mind, twelve factors and no wanting [C029-P:L31–L55] — is not used at all, because the digest restricts it to the liberated and nobody on camera may be framed as having it.

The digest's usable material here is two absences and one constant. The constant: the seven universals appear in every mind without exception, and there is no mind in which they do not occur [C025-P:L47; C025-M:L5]. The first absence: the ten sense-consciousnesses are the weakest resultants and get only those seven, the remaining forty-five factors not occurring, so at bare sensing there is no decision, no drive and no wish [C025-P:L59]. The second absence, and the one this film is actually built on: effort does not arise in sixteen of the rootless minds, and the reason the Pradeepika gives is that they come about by the natural order of mind, without effort [C025-P:L75]. A machine whose correct behaviour is unwilled is the plainest possible picture of that, and it is why the film can be about a tower rather than about anyone tending it. The digest's warnings are the reason the film refuses its own obvious reading. Energy, passion and decisiveness are not virtues in this framework and appear equally in harmful minds, so nothing here — not the engineers named in beat 2, not the authority that runs the light, not anyone who has ever worked in it — is praised for effort, and beat 5 says the framework hands out no marks for it. The absence of desire-to-act in rootless minds does not mean desire is bad [C025-P:L87], and the film never suggests it. The dropping of applied thought and joy in higher absorptions is a specific claim about absorption and is not used here at all, in particular not as an analogy for a well-maintained machine needing no attention. And the memorisation numbers stay off the screen.

The digest gives the episode at full length and, uniquely among the four, it gives the film its physical hook. For the fullest eye-door process the Pradeepika requires four things to be very strong at once — the eye's sensitivity, the visible object, light, and attention — and only then do seventeen moments run: past life-continuum, wavering, arrest, five-door adverting, eye-consciousness, receiving, investigating, determining, seven of impulsion, two of registration, after which the life-continuum resumes [C041-P:L25; C041-P:L29–L48; C041-P:L48; C041-M:L5–L11]. Light is one of the four conditions and the only one that has ever been manufactured, which is why this concept belongs on this location rather than being decorated by it; the same pattern runs at the other four doors [C041-P:L52–L54]. The Margaya adds the detail beat 1's long hold depends on: the moment counted first in the process is a life-continuum moment that the object did not strike, included only because it passed immediately before [C041-M:L9]. The digest's warnings are honoured without exception. The seventeen moments are not a neuroscience timing and no figure in milliseconds, and no comparison with the five-second flash period, is offered anywhere — the flash is a clock for the viewer and never a model of a mind-moment. Receiving, investigating and determining are never played as slow deliberate steps. The self-help line about the pause between stimulus and response is not used, since the digest notes the text says only that impulsion is wholesome, unwholesome or functional and never uses the word choice [C041-P:L46; C041-M:L7]. And the digest's correction is kept in view: what the sources deny is a separate seer standing behind the seeing, not that anything is really seen — so the film never says a ship was not seen, or that seeing is an illusion. The one claim the digest flags for expert checking, that the eye's sensitive matter arises and ceases with the object [C041-P:L56], is not used.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the working part of a thing can be a tiny fraction of the thing, and that the rest is not idleness but the condition of the working part being right. The sources say it about mind: two of the fourteen jobs happen once in a life, the background job happens more than anything else and is never noticed, and the doing sits in a short run of moments near the end. A building that has been kept in the surveyed position, at the surveyed height, on a fixed period, for well over a century, in order to be correct for a few seconds at a time, makes the proportion visible without anyone having to believe anything. What the viewer should not take away is that this is a lesson in patience or attention. It is a fact about how much of anything is waiting.
what_must_be_real: The light is a working aid to navigation and is treated as one: nothing is switched on, off, turned, timed, obscured or repositioned for a shot, and no light, lamp, reflector or beam is added, simulated, composited or graded into existence. The flash period on screen is the real period. Ships in frame are ships that were going past anyway; none is hailed, waited for or lit, and no vessel's name, flag, track or identity is shown or used. If the optic no longer rotates, the film does not pretend it does and the beam shot is simply absent. The long shots are really long — the whole treatment is a refusal to cut for pace, and a shot that is shortened in the edit because nothing is happening in it has given the film away. No person in frame is an exhibit. There are or have been staff here and at least one keeper's routine is documented in print, including a family succession and a fixed number of climbs a day; the film does not use it, does not build a beat on anybody's routine, names nobody, and presents nobody as patient, dutiful, solitary or watchful — the camera cannot show which mental factor is present and the digests say so. Nobody who cannot meaningfully refuse a camera appears, and that includes any employee whose refusal would be awkward with their employer; if the only way to film inside is with staff in shot, the interior is dropped. The colonial record is recorded and not adjudicated: imported British granite at the southern tip of this island is a fact, and the voice neither enjoys the irony nor admires the achievement. The point carries a much older and unrelated religious history that is not this film's subject and appears nowhere in the voice, the framing or the captions. Nothing about the sea, the weather or the season is arranged, and no seaward shot is attempted in a sea state the boat cannot take.
position_hint: closing: it is the group's plainest statement of proportion and its most austere piece of cinema, and it also states the group's limit — that the sources put the weight in the response and describe nobody standing behind it. It should come after the films that take the early stages apart, and it wants to be the last thing in the group because it ends on a refusal rather than a revelation.
risks: Making the tower a metaphor for mindfulness, vigilance, watchfulness or steadiness of character. The digests license none of it: C025 says outright that energy and decisiveness are not virtues in this framework and turn up equally in harmful minds, and C034's background function is described as unfelt, not as attentive. This is the single risk the film is most likely to fail on, because the image invites it.

Letting the long holds read as contemplative or meditative rather than as duration. The film is measuring how much of a thing is waiting; it is not offering a mood, and the digest forbids presenting the sequence as something a viewer could slow down and watch in themselves when the source says countless moments pass in a finger-snap [C034-P:L37].

Turning any person here into a character. A named keeper's routine is already in print and it is exactly the material this series does not use; building a beat on a real person's rounds would break the floor whatever the narration said.

Adjudicating the colonial record. Granite selected in Scotland and Cornwall and shipped to the far end of an empire is recorded as a layer. It is not an irony to enjoy and not an achievement to admire, and the voice does neither.

Letting the point's much older religious history into the film. It is a real and important history, two other films on the slate already deal with colonial destruction of religious sites, and a third would be a pattern rather than a subject. It is held to a single factual clause in the historical thread and appears nowhere else.
Treating the five-second flash as a model of a mind-moment, or offering any millisecond figure for the seventeen moments, which the C041 digest rules out.
Using the language of choice for the impulsion burst, when the digest says neither extract uses it and the text says only wholesome, unwholesome or functional [C041-P:L46].
Using the slogan about freedom living in the gap between stimulus and response, which borrows the shape of the sources and adds a claim they do not make.
Narrating the background current as a subconscious or a hidden true self, or borrowing rebirth-linking as a metaphor for a fresh start. Nothing in this film is a beginning.
Carrying the Pradeepika's link between weak rebirth-producing action and being born blind or deaf [C034-P:L47] into the film in any form.
Letting 'rootless minds are weak' [C029-P:L29] land on a person, a workforce or a nation. It is a count of factors and beat 6 says so.
Putting any factor count or memorisation number on screen as though it were a measurement.

Filming on restricted ground without written permission, or in a way that could affect a working navigational light. This is not a monument; a crew that gets in anyone's way here is interfering with shipping safety.
Building the film on interior access or on the beam in air, both of which may not exist. The treatment has to survive refusal at the gate and a static optic, and it is written so that it does.

Repeating the slate: IDEA-0105 is already a lighthouse film, an offshore granite tower on a reef reached by boat, and its argument is about who the light is for. This one is a shore tower, is built on held frames and duration rather than on isolation, and its argument is about the ratio of waiting to working. If both films are made they must not share a single shot type, and if only one can be made that is a real decision rather than an oversight.
District concentration: three films on the slate are already in this district. That is a slate-level question, not a fault in this film, and it is flagged rather than solved here.
drop_if: Filming anywhere on the point, including from outside the compound wall, cannot be done without a permission that is not forthcoming, or could affect the light's service.
The only way to make the film is with staff in frame who cannot meaningfully refuse.
The optic no longer produces a flash of any kind, or the light has been discontinued, in which case the film has no clock and no subject.
The long holds cannot be kept — if the piece can only be made watchable by cutting for pace, it is a different film and should be a different film.
A seaward angle turns out to be the only way to make the tower read, and no boat can be established for the season in which the sea allows it.

connections.note: The group opens on thirty machines turning to face a wind they cannot yet use, and closes on one machine whose whole existence is being correct for a few seconds at a time. Both are films about the part before and around the output rather than the output.

Two films about the long quiet stretch rather than the event: one about the stretch after a single sound, one about the stretch on either side of a few seconds of use. Different senses, different landscapes, and neither of them cuts for pace.

Both films are lighthouses and the overlap is recorded rather than hidden. IDEA-0105 is an offshore tower on a reef, reached by boat, and its subject is a light kept for people who will never be met. This one stands on the shore, is filmed entirely from static positions at night, and its subject is the proportion between the seconds of use and everything else. They must not share a visual approach, and if the slate can only carry one lighthouse, this note is where the choice starts.

selection.reason: It gives the group its proportion — a very long nothing, a short burst — in a single object, it is the only film in the group built on long takes of nothing happening, and it is the only one of the sixteen candidates that carries a verified historical story. It also states the sources' limit rather than papering over it.

review.note: Rewritten 2026-09-26 onto the lighthouse at the island's southernmost point, keeping the title and the structure of the previous version and replacing everything else. The old film — a dry-season drinking-water round, with coloured plastic pots standing on a red road all day and everything happening in the four minutes after a tanker stopped — went for two separate reasons, and both of them are the reason this version exists. First, monoculture: all sixteen films in this group were working places and not one of them carried a historical story, and a group cannot be a monoculture, so the replacement had to be a built thing with a documented record rather than another trade. Second, and more particular, exposure: that film put a camera on villagers queuing for drinking water in a drought, which is hardship, and the floor is explicit that livelihoods are not destinies and that nobody in frame is an exhibit. The excellent part of it was its shape — a very long wait, a short arrival, a few minutes that carry everything — and the shape survives the move intact; the exposure does not, because the new subject is a machine and the waiting belongs to a building rather than to anyone's morning. The film is now bound to a verified historical thread: a tower designed by Sir James Nicholas Douglass and built by a William Douglass of the Imperial Lighthouse Service, begun in November 1887, reported first lit ceremonially on 8 February 1890 and separately recorded as completed and commissioned in March 1890, built of brick and steel imported from England on granite selected at the Dalbeattie quarries in Scotland and at Penryn in Cornwall, paid for out of the dues of two reef lighthouses, fitted with one of only four hyperradiant Chance Brothers lenses in the island's lights, standing 49 m with a focal plane of 47 m and the tallest lighthouse in the country, still a working aid to navigation under a national ports authority, and still flashing white every five seconds about twelve nautical miles inside a lane that carries more than forty thousand vessels a year. The binding is structural, not poetic: C034's census puts one rebirth-linking mind and one death mind in a whole life, makes the life-continuum the most abundant and the least noticed thing that happens, and puts the doing of action in a short run of moments — which is the specification of a landfall light, whose output is a few seconds per ship and whose remaining existence is keeping that output correct. C041 supplies the episode at full length and names light among the four conditions that must all be strong at once, the only one of them anybody has ever had to build. C029 and C025 supply the neutral workforce underneath, including the Pradeepika's flat reason that these early minds arise without effort, by the order of mind. The one reading the film refuses throughout is the obvious one: the lighthouse is not a metaphor for mindfulness, vigilance or steadiness, the digests license no such move, and the last line of the film says that a light which has not failed is a fact about maintenance. Treatment is the group's most austere and shares nothing with the other fifteen: one vertical structure, an open horizon, night, static frames held for minutes at a time, and a deliberate refusal to cut for pace. Access is the live problem and is written as one — this is restricted working ground, reports of whether the tower may be entered flatly contradict each other, drone permission is treated as doubtful, and the film is built so that it survives being refused at the gate, refused the air and finding a static LED where a rotating lens used to be. Concepts were re-read from the digests and not inherited: the four links are rewritten from scratch, every bearing does_not_transfer line is carried into a link or a risk, and every citation was checked against the source lines it carries as well as against the digest evidence. No concept added or removed. The town's own older history, including the destruction of a major temple there in the sixteenth century, is held to a single factual clause in what_is_certain and appears nowhere else, because two other films on the slate already deal with colonial destruction of religious sites. A connections entry records the overlap with the slate's other lighthouse film.

suggested_location.why_here: It is the only candidate that supplies the concept and the cinema in the same object, and it is a built thing with a documented record in a group that had none. The concept first: this is a landfall light whose whole reason for existing is the few seconds in which a particular vessel is in a particular place, and whose remaining existence — a century and a third of it — is spent being exactly where it was surveyed, at exactly the height it was built, flashing on exactly the period it was given. C034's census says the same thing about mind: one birth-linking moment and one death moment in a whole life, a background function that happens more than anything else and is never felt, and the doing of anything in a short run at the end. The proportion is not an analogy here; it is what the engineering was for. The cinema second: one white vertical object, seven floors and 196 steps of it, standing alone on black rock at the end of an island, with the horizon open through more than half a circle and nothing else tall within sight. At night that gives a black frame with a flash in it every five seconds, which is the premise of the whole treatment — static frames held for minutes, no cutting for pace, and a viewer who can feel the duration. And the sea is not empty: the main east–west lane of this ocean runs about twelve nautical miles south of the point and carries more than forty thousand commercial vessels a year, so a single held shot can contain the tower doing nothing and a ship crossing the frame for two or three minutes, which is the film's argument in one image. Nothing in the frame is anybody's hardship, nobody has to be in it, and the object is indifferent to being filmed.

historical_thread.story:
The tower on this point was built by the British at the end of the eighteen-eighties, as one of a small group of major landfall lights put up around the island in the second half of the nineteenth century. It was designed by Sir James Nicholas Douglass, the engineer-in-chief to Trinity House who had been knighted for the fourth Eddystone lighthouse, and it was built by a William Douglass of the Imperial Lighthouse Service. Which William Douglass is genuinely unsettled and matters, because both candidates are plausible: James's brother William (1831–1923) had already spent years in Ceylon as executive engineer on the Great Basses Reef tower, which was designed by James, begun in 1870 and lit in 1873, and then on the Little Basses tower, which came into service in 1878; James's son William Tregarthen Douglass (1857–1913) has this lighthouse listed among his works with the dates 1889–1890, between Round Island in the Isles of Scilly and Cape Leeuwin in Western Australia. Construction is recorded as commencing in November 1887. Amazinglanka and the popular Sri Lankan accounts say the light was first lit ceremonially on 8 February 1890; the standard reference sentence, sourced to Rajpal Kumar de Silva's 19th Century Newspaper Engravings of Ceylon, says it was completed and commissioned in March 1890; and the encyclopaedic categories file it under lighthouses completed in 1889.

None of the material is local. The bricks and the steel were imported from England, and the granite was supplied from the quarries at Dalbeattie in Kirkcudbrightshire, Scotland and at Penryn in Cornwall — the same pattern as the Basses towers twenty years earlier, whose first stone was also quarried in Scotland and carried out by steamer. The combined cost of erecting this lighthouse and Barberyn on the west coast was £30,000, and it was paid for out of the dues collected at the Basses lighthouses, so this tower was funded by ships passing two other towers.

The optic was the most ambitious thing available. This was one of a limited number of lighthouses in the world designed to house the large hyperradiant Fresnel lenses that became available at the end of the nineteenth century, and four of those lenses went into Ceylon lights, all of them made by Chance Brothers in England. Of the thirty-three hyper-radial lenses ever installed, only a handful are thought to survive intact and in place in their towers anywhere. The tower is an octagonal brick structure, white with fourteen two-panel yellow windows, 49 m (161 ft) tall, with a focal plane of 47 m (154 ft), seven floors and 196 steps to the top. It is described as the tallest lighthouse in Sri Lanka and, in a claim repeated everywhere and sourced nowhere, as one of the tallest in South-East Asia. Its light is a white flash every five seconds with a range of 28 nautical miles, and it carries the international numbers ARLHS SLI-001, Admiralty F0836 and NGA 27276.

It has never stopped being a working aid to navigation, and the record of it is a record of maintenance rather than of events. It was modernised in 2000 with a Differential GPS installation and computer-linked to the other major lights around the coast. A Lighthouse Digest feature from the early 2000s describes the interior walls and stairways being repainted every fortnight and the exterior every five years, and a keeper who had held the post for twenty years and whose father had held it before him, climbing the tower four times a day to work the lights and send radio signals. In May 2017 the ministry responsible for ports is reported to have opened the lighthouse as a visitor attraction. And the rotating lens is reported to have been removed in 2020 and replaced with a static flashing LED, which has considerably reduced the light's range — a statement that appears in the standard reference article with no source attached to it.

The sea it exists for is not quiet. The main east–west shipping lane between Europe and the Far East passes some twelve nautical miles south of this point, carrying more than forty thousand commercial vessels a year, and since the 2010s there has been a sustained international argument — taken to the International Maritime Organization by shipping and conservation bodies — about moving the traffic separation scheme further offshore, because the existing lane runs through the feeding grounds of a resident population of blue whales. In December 2004 the tsunami that struck the island's east coast refracted around this point before inundating the south-west, and the shore either side of it was surveyed for damage afterwards; nothing found in this research records damage to the tower itself.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
The concept earns this location structurally, which is the test, and the work is done by C034's census rather than by any resemblance.

Start with what the life-continuum function actually is, because the film stands or falls on it. The Pradeepika gives it a job description with no poetry in it: the function that supports the unbroken continuation of the existence [C034-P:L65]. After the birth-linking moment has arisen and ceased, the same resultant mind takes the same object and goes on arising, as a limb of holding the mind-series together, until the end of that life; at all times when no mind is arising that takes an object from the present life, this is what is occurring; when a new object does turn up, this mind breaks, a cognitive process runs on the new object, and when the process is over the series starts again; and while it is present no other mind arises. The same nineteen minds that link a birth perform it [C034-P:L67], its object is inherited from the previous life and the source calls it unapparent [C034-P:L73], and the Margaya does the arithmetic outright: in one life a person has exactly one birth-linking mind and exactly one death mind; what arises abundantly in beings is the life-continuum; and its arising is not felt [C034-M:L41]. So of the fourteen functions, two happen once each in a whole life, and the one that accounts for the overwhelming majority of a mind-stream is the one whose entire job is accurate continuation and which nobody ever notices. The same line then puts the doing of actions, and merit and demerit, in the impulsion moments.

Now the building. Its purpose is not to be looked at and not to shine; its purpose is that when a particular vessel is at a particular bearing and distance, the answer it gives is already correct. More than forty thousand ships a year pass about twelve nautical miles south of it. For each one of them the useful part of what this tower does lasts minutes at most, and for many of them, in an era of satellite fixing, seconds of confirmation. Everything else it does — standing in the surveyed position, holding a focal plane of forty-seven metres, keeping a five-second period, being repainted inside every fortnight and outside every five years, being powered from the mains with a generator behind it — is not idleness and is not preparation for something better. It is the condition of the brief thing being right. That is a machine whose output is almost entirely waiting, and the waiting is load-bearing. The history is what makes this checkable rather than assertable: everything decided in 1887 was decided for duration. Granite was selected at Dalbeattie and at Penryn rather than quarried within sight of the site; brick and steel came from England; the money came from the dues of two other lighthouses on a different coast; and the lens fitted was the largest class ever made, built for landfall. Nobody spends £30,000 of somebody else's dues and two shiploads of Scottish and Cornish stone on a few seconds per ship unless the seconds are the whole point and the permanence is how you get them.

C041 supplies the episode at its full length and one piece of physical luck that no other location on the slate can offer. For the fullest kind of seeing the Pradeepika requires four things to be very strong at the same moment — the eye's sensitivity, the visible object, light, and attention — and only then does the seventeen-moment process run [C041-P:L25; C041-P:L29–L48], ending with the life-continuum resuming [C041-P:L48]. Of those four conditions, light is the only one that has ever been manufactured. A lighthouse is not a symbol of seeing; it is a factory for one of seeing's four named conditions, and that is a much smaller and much more accurate claim. The Margaya adds the detail the film's opening hold depends on: the first moment counted in the process is a life-continuum moment that the object did not strike at all, included in the count only because it passed immediately before the striking [C041-M:L9]. A frame of a dark sea, one flash, and no ship in it is that moment, and it belongs to the process.

C029 and C025 supply the workforce that runs under all of it and, more importantly, they are why the colonial record can be in this film without being argued about. The seven universals run in every mind without exception [C025-P:L47; C025-M:L5]. The ten sense-consciousnesses get only those seven, the other forty-five factors not occurring, so at bare sensing there is no decision, no drive and no wish [C025-P:L59]. Effort does not arise in sixteen of the rootless minds at all, and the reason the Pradeepika gives is that they come about by the natural order of mind, without effort [C025-P:L75]. The eighteen rootless minds carry no unwholesome and no beautiful factor and are therefore called weak [C029-P:L29], the five groupings differ from one another by a factor at a time [C029-P:L31–L55], the barest of them has only the seven and nothing else [C029-P:L35], and not one of them contains a desire to act [C029-M:L3; C025-P:L87]. That is a neutral machinery that is the same under every state: the same seven factors under an empire's lighthouse service and under a national ports authority, the same absence of wanting in the receiving stages whoever owns the tower. Which is exactly the licence for recording that the stone came from Scotland and Cornwall and the money came from other ships' dues, and for adjudicating none of it.

And the same digests are what stop the film becoming the thing it most easily could. C025 says energy, passion and decisiveness are not virtues in this framework and appear equally in harmful minds; C034 says the background moments are never felt and that countless moments pass in a finger-snap [C034-P:L37]; C041 says the text never uses the word choice [C041-P:L46]. So there is no reading available here in which the lighthouse is steadfast, or vigilant, or an example of anything. A mental factor is not a virtue and a building is not a character. The film's last line is the one the sources actually support: the light has not failed because it has been maintained.
what_is_certain: The lighthouse stands on Dondra Head, the southernmost point of Sri Lanka, in Matara District, Southern Province, approximately 6 km south-east of Matara town. It is operated and maintained by the Sri Lanka Ports Authority and is an active aid to navigation.

It was designed by Sir James Nicholas Douglass, and the construction is credited to a William Douglass of the Imperial Lighthouse Service. Construction commenced in November 1887, on the authority of Rajpal Kumar de Silva, 19th Century Newspaper Engravings of Ceylon – Sri Lanka (Serendib Publications, 1998).
All the building materials including the bricks and the steel were imported from England, and the granite was supplied from the quarries at Dalbeattie in Scotland and Penryn in Cornwall.
The combined cost of erecting this lighthouse and the Barberyn lighthouse was £30,000, and it was paid for by dues collected at the Basses lighthouses.

The tower is an octagonal brick tower with balcony and lantern, white with fourteen two-panel yellow windows, of seven floors, with 196 steps to the top. It is 49 m (161 ft) high with a focal plane of 47 m (154 ft), and it is Sri Lanka's tallest lighthouse.
The light characteristic is a white flash every five seconds and the range is given as 28 nautical miles. The international references are ARLHS SLI-001, Admiralty F0836 and NGA 27276.

This was one of a limited number of lighthouses designed to house the large hyperradiant Fresnel lenses that became available at the end of the nineteenth century; four of those lenses were used in Sri Lankan lights, all made by Chance Brothers in England. Hyper-radial lenses were the largest ever put into use and were installed in roughly two dozen major landfall beacons worldwide, of which only a handful are thought to survive intact in place.

It was modernised in 2000 with the introduction of a Differential Global Positioning System and is computer-linked to the other major lighthouses around the coast. It is described as one of four international lighthouses in Sri Lanka.

James Nicholas Douglass (1826–1898) was engineer-in-chief to Trinity House and was knighted for the fourth Eddystone lighthouse. His brother William Douglass (1831–1923) was executive engineer for the Great Basses Reef lighthouse in Ceylon, designed by James, whose first stone was quarried in Scotland and laid in December 1870 and whose light was installed in March 1873, and then for the Little Basses Reef lighthouse, operational in 1878; he was afterwards engineer-in-chief to the Commissioners of Irish Lights from 1878 to 1900. James's son William Tregarthen Douglass (1857–1913) has Dondra Head listed among his works with the dates 1889–1890.

The main east–west shipping route passes about twelve nautical miles south of Dondra Head, and more than forty thousand commercial vessels are reported to travel it annually. Proposals to move the traffic separation scheme further offshore, to reduce ship strikes on a resident blue whale population, have been put to the International Maritime Organization by shipping and conservation bodies.

In the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami the waves that struck the east coast refracted around Dondra Head before inundating the south-west of the island, and the shore between Weligama and Dondra was surveyed for damage afterwards.

The town at this point, Devinuwara or Dondra, is an ancient temple port whose name means city of the gods, whose oldest recorded mention is taken to be a rock inscription of Nissankamalla (1187–1196) at Dambulla, and whose major temple complex was destroyed in 1587 by a Portuguese force under Thomé de Sousa d'Arronches; that history is not this film's subject and is recorded here only because a crew working on the point will encounter its surviving granite pillars.
what_is_disputed: The completion and first-lighting dates. Sri Lankan popular and heritage accounts, including AmazingLanka, say the lighthouse was built in 1889 and first lit ceremonially on 8 February 1890. The standard reference sentence, sourced to de Silva 1998, says it was completed and commissioned in March 1890. Encyclopaedic categorisation files it under lighthouses completed in 1889, and William Tregarthen Douglass's list of works dates it 1889–1890. The start date of November 1887 is the only one that is not in dispute. A ceremonial first lighting in February and a commissioning in March are not necessarily in conflict, but no source consulted reconciles them and none gives a primary reference for the February date.

Which William Douglass built it. The construction credit reads 'William Douglass of the Imperial Lighthouse Service' and the encyclopaedia's link resolves to William Tregarthen Douglass (1857–1913), James's son, whose own works list includes it. But James's brother William Douglass (1831–1923) had already built both Basses towers in Ceylon and is the more experienced candidate for a tropical landfall light. Nothing found here settles it, and the film names no William: the voice says 'a Douglass built it'.

The height figures. 49 m / 161 ft is the figure in the reference literature and in the navigational lists. Sri Lankan accounts commonly give 160 feet, and a Lighthouse Digest feature gives 150 feet. AmazingLanka gives the focal height as 153 metres, which cannot be right for a 160-foot tower and is presumably 153 feet; the navigational figure is 47 m / 154 ft.

'One of the tallest in South-East Asia.' This claim is repeated in almost every account and is sourced in none of them. Sri Lanka is not in South-East Asia, and no comparative list of South or South-East Asian lighthouse heights was located. That it is the tallest in Sri Lanka is supported by the lighthouse reference literature; the regional claim is recorded as a claim.

The flash period. Every navigational source gives Fl W 5s, a white flash every five seconds. A Lighthouse Digest feature from the early 2000s describes the main light as yellow and going off every six seconds, and mentions forty smaller lights rotating through the night. The film's clock is the five-second period and it has to be verified on site before a single frame is shot, because the entire treatment runs on it.

Whether the original rotating hyperradiant lens is still there. The statement that the rotating lens was removed in 2020 and replaced by a static flashing LED, considerably reducing the range, appears in the standard reference article with no citation attached, and no independent confirmation was found. If it is true, the beam sweeping through the air does not exist and the shot list must not assume it; if it is false, a hyper-radial survivor is in that lantern and the close work is a different proposition. Nothing in the research settles it, and the film is written so that it works either way.

Whether the tower may be entered. The lighthouse reference directory records the site as open and the tower as open daily, and notes that in May 2017 the ministry responsible for ports opened the lighthouse as a tourist attraction. Other accounts say visitors may walk the compound but not climb, that special permission must be obtained from the Sri Lanka Ports Authority head office in Colombo to reach the balcony, that entry to the compound was once banned and was later allowed, and visitor reports from December 2017 say the lighthouse itself was not open. The position is genuinely unknown and may vary month to month.

Staffing. A Lighthouse Digest feature from the early 2000s describes a named resident keeper of twenty years' standing who had succeeded his father and climbed the tower four times a day. Whether the light is still attended, and by how many people, was not established, and the film does not depend on the answer: no person's routine is a beat and nobody is filmed who cannot refuse.

Any interruption in the light's service. No record of the light failing, being extinguished, or being damaged — by the 2004 tsunami or otherwise — was found, and an absence of records is not a record of continuity. The claim that the light has never failed is therefore not made; what is made is the narrower and better claim that it has been maintained.
The geology of the point itself. It is a low rocky headland and is repeatedly described as rock rather than sand, but no source consulted names the rock type, and the film asserts nothing about it.

what_to_film: The night hold, which is the film: one static wide frame, tower left or right of centre, open black sea filling the rest, the flash every five seconds, run for as long as the card will take. Several of these, on different nights and from different distances, and none of them shortened in the edit.
The switch-on at dusk and the switch-off at dawn, each in one unbroken static frame that starts well before and ends well after. These are the two events of the day and they are not built up to.

The whole tower in daylight from the ground, static, at three distances: the full column with the rock and the surf at its foot, the middle third with the windows, and the lantern and gallery from directly below. Long lens for the top, so the compression makes the height legible without a drone.

Surfaces, macro, static, one shot at a time: the joints between the imported granite blocks, salt drying on painted brick, paint over paint, a rusted bolt head, glass. This is the only part of the film that is about the nineteenth century, and it is carried entirely by texture rather than by narration.

Ships far out in the light's arc, at night and at dusk, in frames that are already running before the ship enters and keep running after it has gone. No ship is identified and none is waited for beyond the length of an ordinary hold.
The horizon itself, at several points around the point, to establish that the sea fills more than half a circle from here: one slow pan only if the film needs it, otherwise a set of static frames.

The beam sweeping through air over the water — conditional, and carried as such. It exists only if the optic still rotates and only in air thick enough to show it. If the light is a static LED this shot does not exist and nothing replaces it.

The interior — conditional on written permission, which may not come: the painted stairwell as a vertical receding shape, the window embrasures, the lantern room, the optic. Filmed with nobody in frame. If entry is refused the film loses none of its beats, because every beat is written from outside.

The working fabric from outside the tower: the compound wall, the service door, cable and conduit runs, a generator housing, the coconut palms bent inland. Static, plain, no commentary in the framing.

A seaward angle of the tower from the water — conditional and carrying its dependency. It is only attempted in the calm season, only from a boat whose availability and licensing have been established in advance, and never in a sea state the boat cannot take. The tower reads perfectly well from the ground and the film does not need this shot.
suggested_location.access: By road: the southern coast road to Matara and then about 6 km south-east through Dondra town to the point; the lighthouse is at the end of a short lane and is visible from a distance. Getting to the point is easy and getting into the tower may be impossible. This is a working aid to navigation on restricted ground, owned and run by the Sri Lanka Ports Authority, and the reports contradict each other flatly: the lighthouse reference directory records the site as open and the tower as open daily and says the ministry responsible for ports opened it as a visitor attraction in May 2017, while other accounts say the compound was once closed and later opened, that visitors may walk the base but not climb, and that special permission from the Ports Authority head office in Colombo is needed to reach the balcony; visitor reports from as recently as late 2017 say the tower itself was shut. Nobody has been approached and no permission has been sought. Plan on three separate permissions and expect to be refused at least one: written clearance from the Ports Authority for any filming on the compound, a separate clearance for entering and climbing the tower, and, if any seaward angle is wanted, a boat with its own licensing. Assume also that filming may be conditioned or stopped on the day, because a navigational light in service outranks a film crew. Every beat in this film is written to be shootable from public ground outside the compound wall: if the crew never gets past the gate, the night holds, the switch-on, the switch-off, the long lens work, the ships and the surfaces of the lower courses all still exist, and the film survives intact. Drone: doubtful and treated as such. A lighthouse is an obvious aerial subject and an equally obvious restricted one — it is state infrastructure on a coastal point, Sri Lankan drone flight requires civil aviation permission, and permission over a port authority installation should be assumed to be refused until it is granted in writing. No beat depends on an aerial. A tower reads perfectly well from the ground, and a long lens from a distance does the height better than an aerial does.
suggested_location.best_time: Night, which is the film, and specifically the dark of the moon for the flash against black and a moonlit night for the tower to have a profile in the same frame as its own light. Dusk and dawn for the two events. Season: the calm months between the monsoons, roughly December to March on this coast, for clear air, a workable sea and any prospect at all of a boat; the south-west monsoon from about May to September gives a heavier and more interesting sea and takes the seaward angle away. Whether the optic still rotates has to be checked before the trip is booked, because one conditional shot depends on it.

suggested_location.research_note: All of this is desk research by web search, carried out on 26 September 2026, and none of it has been checked on the ground or against a printed edition. The coordinates are the reference coordinates given for the lighthouse itself (5°55′16.71″N 80°35′38.73″E), converted to decimal. The construction dates, the designer, the builder's name, the imported brick and steel, the Dalbeattie and Penryn granite, the £30,000 shared cost and its funding from the Basses dues all rest on the reference article's citation of Rajpal Kumar de Silva, 19th Century Newspaper Engravings of Ceylon – Sri Lanka (1998), which was not read; the ceremonial first-lighting date of 8 February 1890 comes from Sri Lankan heritage sites and no primary reference for it was located. The height, focal plane, characteristic, range and international numbers were cross-read between the reference article and the standard lighthouse directory, which agree; the Sri Lankan popular figures of 160 and 150 feet and the 153-metre focal height disagree with them and are recorded as disputed rather than reconciled. The two Williams Douglass were checked against both encyclopaedia articles and the biographical memoir hosted by the United States Lighthouse Society; the son's works list names this lighthouse and the brother's Ceylon experience is documented, and the identification is left open. The statement that the rotating lens was removed in 2020 and replaced with a static LED is uncited in the reference article and could not be confirmed anywhere else; it is the single most consequential unknown in the file, because one conditional shot depends on it, and the treatment is written so that the film works without that shot. The keeper described in the early-2000s Lighthouse Digest feature is recorded here only in order to state that the film does not use him: he is named in that article, he is not named here, and no beat rests on anybody's routine. Access is contradictory between sources and unverified: the directory says the tower is open daily, other accounts require written permission from the Ports Authority head office in Colombo, and no approach has been made to anyone. Drone permission is unverified and treated as likely to be refused. No boat has been identified for any seaward angle and none is assumed. Nothing was found recording damage to the tower in the 2004 tsunami, and that absence is recorded as an absence rather than as continuity. The shipping figures — the lane about twelve nautical miles south and more than forty thousand vessels a year — come from shipping-industry and Sri Lankan press sources and from the IMO filing on the traffic separation scheme, and were not checked against a hydrographic publication. All four images were confirmed to exist through the Commons query API before their URLs were written; all four show this lighthouse rather than a look-alike or a landform. The town's own older history, including the 1587 destruction of its temple complex, was researched far enough to state one factual clause accurately and then deliberately left alone: it is not this film's subject and it appears in one clause in what_is_certain and nowhere else in this record.

unknowns: Whether any permission to film on the compound will be granted at all. This is restricted working ground under a national ports authority, nobody has been approached, and refusal is a realistic outcome. The film is written so that every beat is shootable from public ground outside the wall.

Whether the tower may be entered or climbed. The sources flatly contradict each other — one directory records it as open daily and notes a 2017 opening as a visitor attraction, others require written permission from the ports authority's head office in the capital, and visitor reports say it has been shut — and the position may change month to month. No interior shot is load-bearing.

Whether the original rotating hyperradiant lens is still in the lantern, or whether it was removed in 2020 and replaced by a static LED. The claim is uncited and unconfirmed. It decides whether a beam in air exists to be filmed, and it is the one thing that must be checked before the trip is booked.

Whether the flash period is still five seconds. Every navigational source says it is; one magazine account says six. The whole treatment is timed to the real period and the real period has not been observed.

Whether anyone is stationed at the light, and whether a documented keeper's post still exists. The film does not depend on the answer and will not build a beat on it either way, but it decides whether there is anyone on the compound whose consent is needed.
Drone permission over a port authority installation on a coastal point. Treated as doubtful and probably refused; no shot in the film requires an aerial.
Whether a boat can be established for the one seaward angle, in a season when the sea allows it. None has been identified, the shot carries its dependency, and it is not attempted otherwise.
Whether the point is quiet enough at night to hold shots of several minutes without interruption. It is a visited place a few hundred metres from a town, and the treatment depends on duration.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is proposed by Claude from desk research and is unverified. No scene or shot is decided here.
